# Purpose, Structure, Priorities

# Rotational Interrupt Team (RIT)

# Purpose

The Rotational Interrupt Team (RIT) serves to focus interruptions to developer time into a single group on a rotating basis. There are many sources of interruption, from bugs and escalations to component readiness and CI disasters that we cannot plan for, and typically would be routed directly to an SME, taking them away from their feature work and other planned priorities.

By creating a rotational team responsibility, we can now better plan for interruptions and adjust development capacity based on the rotation.

# Structure

On a weekly basis, the PIXAA managers will rotate through the RIT Lead role. As RIT Lead, the managers will be responsible for tracking interruptions (see [Priorities](#priorities)) and ensuring that engineers from within their pods are assigned to those interruptions. All pods under a manager are expected to participate in the rotation during their manager's shift as RIT Lead.

The RIT Lead should always be reachable by the **@pixaa-interrupt-lead** slack alias, and their team by the **@pixaa-interrupt-team** slack alias. The [**\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt**](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0B2C9VAHLK) channel is dedicated to RIT communication.

## Schedule

The RIT schedule can be found in [PIXAA RIT Schedule](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KNHoKWgMYyalxtA1ZPBMXQ3yqc6rsgD6qBKs5xJmCcE/edit?gid=0#gid=0). RIT leads must assign team members to the various [rotational roles]() in advance of their rotation starting.

For those interested, the schedule introduces a slip (rather than being consistently ordered every two sprints) so that after a team is on rotation in the first week of the two sprint block, they move to the end of rotation for the next block. This should help mitigate teams repeatedly missing certain rituals or being aligned to specific weeks such as branch week.

# Priorities {#priorities}

The RIT team will handle interruptions from across the org’s scope to minimise unplanned interruptions to pods focusing on feature work. The RIT Lead should be responsible for assigning engineers based on the ordered priorities below.

1. [Customer Escalations](https://source.redhat.com/departments/products_and_global_engineering/gss_openshift/cee_openshift_wiki/how_to_engage_openshift_engineering_rhose_prio_revamp) ([RHOCPPRIO](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/software/c/projects/RHOCPPRIO/issues/))  
2. Component Readiness Failures, both [public](https://sippy.dptools.openshift.org/sippy-ng/component_readiness/main?view=5.0-main) and [QE-internal](https://qe-component-readiness.dptools.openshift.org/sippy-ng/component_readiness/main?view=4.22-qe-main).  
3. The [PIXAA bugs dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023)   
   * Release blocking bugs in the *Release Blockers* panel.  
   * Highest priority bugs from the backlog (e.g CVEs)  
   * Triaging new and pre-pixaa untriaged bugs  
4. Support channels (e.g. slack forums).  **\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt**, the **@pixaa-interrupt-lead** slack alias, and their team by the **@pixaa-interrupt-team** slack alias

# Non-Priorities

The RIT team cannot solve all interrupt issues. Notably:

* The RIT team may not have the expertise to solve all issues that arise during their rotation. It is expected that in some cases they may need to [escalate to an SME](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1T9sXn9w8aZske2KCWtB9b8_X-R9GS6ERhZc46SriFqc/edit?tab=t.wingf7r6kygb#heading=h.prmw8k1s2eez) beyond the RIT team.  
* The RIT team cannot be expected to solve all bugs on the backlog. Bugs vary in priority and the team will pick up the highest priority bugs from the backlog with the time that they have.

# Team Roles

# Rotation Interrupt Team Roles

# RIT Lead

Prior to the RIT shift, the RIT lead (engineering manager) is expected to assign members of their team to the various rotational monitor roles, assuring that each assignee is aware they should pick up this role on the following Monday.  
   
At the beginning of the RIT shift, the RIT lead should review [the ongoing RIT status document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zqQmjpQStnSlQCuxoavDAkNA0NIZmevuGtd0eo7GgfU/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.4uto2atm2tq) (updated by the previous RIT lead Friday EOD previous week). This will detail and highlight any ongoing customer escalations or high priority issues that the RIT Lead should need to be immediately made aware of. 

Slack aliases should have already been updated at the end of the prior RIT shift by the outgoing lead, but the incoming lead should ensure the **@pixaa-interrupt-lead** Slack alias points to themselves, and ensure the **@pixaa-interrupt-team** Slack alias is updated to include their direct engineers. Also ensure Slack aliases for some of the other team roles, including **@ota-monitor** for [the OTA monitor](#ota-monitor).

The RIT Lead is responsible for monitoring the priority inputs, and keeping the RIT status document up to date on a daily basis. The RIT Lead should organise a daily scrum with their team to check in on issues and update the status document to reflect. This document is the source of truth and must be kept up to date to allow the next rotation to understand the status of ongoing issues.

At the end of the RIT shift, the RIT lead should work with their team to understand which issues are suitable for handing over to the next RIT team, and which should not. Any issues where engineers are deeply invested, or are particularly complex, should be continued by the engineer the following week as they return to their usual feature rotation. This avoids the need for continuous context switching and handovers between engineers and provides continuity on complex customer cases.

The RIT status doc should be updated to detail which ongoing issues are to be handed over, and highlight where the RIT lead should focus on their Monday morning. For issues not to be handed over, mark these appropriately.

Finally, the RIT lead should update the lead and team Slack aliases to point to the incoming lead and team members, so any weekend Slack pings are queued up in the incoming team's notification backlog when they start their shift

# RIT Members

At the beginning of the week, RIT members should review the RIT status doc to assess if there are any ongoing issues that they should adopt. If there are, they should assign themselves and start working on the issue. Otherwise they should follow the [RIT Priorities](#priorities) until they find an issue to start working on. This should all be visible in the [PIXAA bugs dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023). 

Depending on timezones, the RIT lead may have assigned them something already, or may want to redirect them to something higher priority once they come online. The RIT [Triage Monitor](#triage-monitor) may also have assigned them bugs during their async triage process.

While RIT members will primarily spend their week looking at bugs, they are NOT responsible for solving every issue. It is important to understand that we have different SMEs spread across the organization and that not every RIT will have the skills to solve every bug. We expect RIT members to act as triage (initial assessment, gathering logs and required artifacts to debug) on every issue, but also be cognizant of their limitations and seek help from/re-assign to SMEs if required. The RIT members will reduce day to day interrupts, but cannot completely prevent them.

During their rotation, it is expected that feature work is paused and the RIT members focus exclusively on the RIT priorities and the bug backlog. However, not all issues can be resolved within the week. RIT members should expect that sufficient complex issues will be carried over to the following week should it not be resolved by EOD Friday. We hope on average this means that interrupts take \~1.5 weeks from an engineer's schedule each rotation, equating to about 25% of our engineering time.

During the Friday scrum, the RIT members and lead will assess which issues should and should not be handed over to the next team.

# Triage Monitor {#triage-monitor}

The weekly Triage monitor will be assigned by the RIT lead prior to the start of the rotation. [Update](#update-a-slack-alias) the **@pixaa-interrupt-bug-triage** alias at the beginning of the rotation.

The triage monitor will take primary responsibility for triaging incoming bugs for the org.  
Throughout the week, they should monitor for [untriaged bugs](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023#v=1&d=25023&rf=019df8d4-fead-7cda-9eea-99b816fd674b&smart=019dfc77-c722-78a4-bba5-5faba824000f:019dfc79-2335-7f6a-84fe-0a35a3963d92;019e0714-b7b0-70f6-afb4-e30e77023e91:019e0715-c022-7ce4-9dc3-d9c8762b836b&g=97428:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97429:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97430:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97432:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97806:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97807:view@019e06bb-a647-70d3-8faf-37dbee373687;97810:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97813:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97816:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64) and follow the triage process below to assign an initial priority and RIT member to continue initial investigation.

For each untriaged bug, the monitor should follow the [bug triage process](#pixaa-bug-triage-process).

# QA Monitor

The weekly QA monitor will be assigned by the RIT lead prior to the start of the rotation. [Update](#update-a-slack-alias) the **@pixaa-interrupt-qa** alias at the beginning of the rotation.

The QA monitor will take primary responsibility for ensuring that bugs that have reached the ON\_QA bug phase are assigned an engineer to move them to Verified.

We expect most bugs to be pre-merge verified before they are merged, in which case the PR will have the `verified` label, and not the `verified-later` label.

Only PRs with the `verified-later` label will need manual verification at this phase. The release controller will comment on the Jira issue to explain this and label the Jira issue with `post-merge-verification`. Any issue that only has linked pre-merge verified PRs will automatically move to verified, and no manual action is needed.

The QA Monitor can use this [dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023#v=1&d=25023&rf=019df8d4-fead-7cda-9eea-99b816fd674b&smart=019e2bcc-ee24-786a-9eac-bee6db0f7a35:019e2bcd-411c-7cd3-89c6-7643e49eab31&g=97428:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97429:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97430:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97432:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97806:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97807:view@019e06bb-a647-70d3-8faf-37dbee373687;97810:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97813:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97816:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64) to filter down to issues that need post-merge verification attention. Filter must be set to “*show manual verification*”. 

When dealing with these type of bugs QA Monitor needs to check if the bug assignee is blocked somehow, if the assignee cannot verify a bug because they lack environment access, the QA Monitor can assist by looking for help across the RIT first, and to the [organization's pods](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1XHWfuJJTTouvQXiApzdiT6H09cwHsDJGbqdzXFl1-4s/edit?usp=sharing) then. For example, almost every pod has an embedded Quality Engineer (QE) who might be able to help grant access or run the automated verifications.

# OTA Monitor {#ota-monitor}

The weekly OTA monitor will be assigned by the RIT lead prior to the start of the rotation. [Update](#update-a-slack-alias) the **@ota-monitor** alias at the beginning of the rotation.

Narrowly, OTA-monitor responsibilities are:

* Check the [triage board](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/18775) once a day, and nudge things along [the UpgradeBlocker flow](https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/tree/master/enhancements/update/update-blocker-lifecycle#summary).  
* Listen for Slack pings for the **@ota-monitor** alias.

The OTA monitor will take responsibility for requesting and assessing impact statements on `UpgradeBlocker` bugs, and for [blocking upgrade edges](https://github.com/openshift/cincinnati-graph-data/pulls) when required.

The process for this role is described in this [enhancement](https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/tree/master/enhancements/update/update-blocker-lifecycle) and the OTA monitor should monitor this [dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/18775). We have a tool for handling OTA tasks; you can find more information [here](#ota-monitor-1).

Watch Cincinnati graph-data activity in [\#osus-graph-data-automation](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C02MX20TV24). If any of the promotions [fail](https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/C02MX20TV24/p1781303538696799), take action as soon as possible; Cincinnati is a time-sensitive pipeline. You can see how to handle failed promotions [here]().

Escalate to the OpenShift Cluster Updates [CCSIG](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bXGksEjpSjnFcrKt3Aln9dIQXF02_jfX5B0tInJChZY/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.zd3xlp469xk0) in [\#forum-ocp-updates](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/CEGKQ43CP) / [\#pixaa-ccsig-openshift-cluster-updates](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0B3ZT5AEG4) if you need support.

# Hive Monitor

The weekly Hive monitor will be assigned by the RIT lead prior to the start of the rotation. [Update](#update-a-slack-alias) the **@pixaa-interrupt-hive** alias at the beginning of the rotation.

## Build and Push OperatorHub Bundles

The Hive monitor is responsible for building and pushing a Hive build to OperatorHub when HCM pushes a production deployment. This can be monitored in the [\#team-hive-info](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0135RY7ZCN) channel: a successful production deployment results in a series of messages like [these](https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/C0135RY7ZCN/p1776871420506419). The HCM coordinated release process can be tracked in more detail in [\#forum-hcm-deployments](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C081W589GRG).  
Before pushing, they must check with QE (nominally Milind Yadav for now) that the pre-promotion smoke tests have been run and completed without issue.

When ready, the Hive monitor should follow this [SOP](https://github.com/openshift/hive-sops/blob/master/sop/PushToOperatorHub.md) to build and push the release. There are some pre-requisites that need to be set up before this can be done, so the Hive monitor should make sure they have these available early in the week.

Note, presently there are some issues with the SOP which [HIVE-3130](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HIVE-3130) aims to fix.

## Monitor \#team-hive-alert For Periodic Failures

Hive's [periodic jobs](https://github.com/openshift/release/blob/main/ci-operator/config/openshift/hive/openshift-hive-master__periodic.yaml) report failures (and sometimes successes) in [\#team-hive-alert](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/CJPQ5BFC7). Failures should be triaged as follows:

- **Infra flakes in setup:** Report in status doc so the subsequent week's run can be validated. This effectively constitutes a missed signal for a week, so we just want next week's monitor to lower the flag on a successful run; or keep it raised if we get another failure. We just don't want to go too long without a green signal.  
- **Infra flakes in post:** If the actual test part of the job succeeded, we treat this as success. If we've been watching this job due to prior failures, we can reset the flag in this scenario.  
- **Failures in the actual test:** Dig in. Usually it's a flake. Sometimes it's not. If not, or if in doubt, open a bug. Either way, note it in the status doc so we can monitor the subsequent week's run.  
    
  Common patterns:  
    
- [Flapping alerts](https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJPQ5BFC7/p1782463193142469) (Failing \-\> Resolved). Note \[RESOLVED\] after \[FIRING\]. If you see one \[FIRING\] for more than, say, a couple hours without self-resolving, then it's probably worth digging into with more urgency.  
- [Cloud credential operator alerts:](https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJPQ5BFC7/p1782437452116149) These can be ignored, and should eventually end up not being routed to the hive alerts channel.

# Slack Monitor {#slack-monitor}

The weekly Slack monitor will be assigned by the RIT lead prior to the start of the rotation. [Update](#update-a-slack-alias) the **@pixaa-interrupt-slack** alias at the beginning of the rotation.

The slack monitor will be the primary triage contact for conversations started in [the slack support channels](#support-channel-handling-\(slack\)). Their role is to ensure that every thread is assigned someone to own it, not to own every thread.

They should use their knowledge of their fellow RIT members to try and find the closest SME with capacity to assist on the thread, leveraging [\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0B2C9VAHLK) as a rally point to highlight the thread and discuss who should own it. All “I need a human” workflow pings from across PIXAA’s channels should be routed to this channel.

RIT members should keep an eye on [\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0B2C9VAHLK) to assist their pod mates with these requests.

# Processes

# Rotation Interrupt Team Processes

The processes outlined here are open to evolution over time and should by no means be considered to be set in stone. While on rotation, RIT members should feel empowered to improve the process as they see fit. Tooling to enable the RIT to be successful should be shared via the [openshift-eng/pixaa](https://github.com/openshift-eng/pixaa) repository.

# RIT Status Tracking

The RIT team should maintain a [weekly status](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1zqQmjpQStnSlQCuxoavDAkNA0NIZmevuGtd0eo7GgfU/edit) during their daily RIT wide standups. Any ongoing issues should be tracked with details of the source of the escalation, assigned engineer and latest updates from the issue.

At the end of the week, the RIT must make a decision on handing over ongoing escalations or whether the engineer is sufficiently deeply involved that they should continue to work the escalation the following week.  
The next RIT lead is expected to pick up these ongoing issues and assign them out to their team early the following week to ensure the issues are not dropped.

# PIXAA Bug Process

To be able to successfully identify which bugs are a priority to work on, the RIT group must triage all incoming bugs. This will be primarily handled by the [Triage Monitor](#triage-monitor) async throughout the week, but should always be covered during the daily sync meeting. This ensures team members can be kept aware of bugs they have been assigned and discuss any bugs the triage monitor has not been able to triage independently.

A triaged bug should be assigned a valid priority, and an engineer to own the initial investigation and potentially take the bug to completion. A triaged bug should **not** be taken out of the New category.

Historically bugs may have been created across a variety of projects, moving forward, we will align on OCPBUGS for all bugs across PIXAA.

## PIXAA bug lifecycle

### New

Bugs are in New by default. In this phase we expect bugs to be triaged for priority and allocated an initial jira assignee for investigation.

The initial assignee should ensure the bug has enough detail and appropriate logs (e.g. through must-gather) to be able to diagnose the issue. They should continue this investigation to the best of their ability until they either 1\) have identified the issue and are ready to start working on a fix or 2\) have exhausted their component knowledge and need to identify an SME to hand the bug to. 

The initial assignee is expected to keep the bug up to date with their findings through regular comments explaining their findings.

If at the end of a rotation the initial assignee has neither started, nor sufficiently explored a bug, they may choose to unassign themselves and have the next RIT rotation assign a new assignee.

### Assigned

Bugs are moved to assigned once the issue has been identified. Moving to assigned implies that the assigned individual will now see this bug to completion. The bug should have been updated by this point with details of the investigation and a summary of what the expected issue is.

The assignee is expected to schedule working on this bug in and around their other assigned, prioritised work.

### Post

The bug now has a proposed fix. RIT members should monitor bugs in Post to identify where they can provide assistance in moving a bug to completion. This may be in the form of PR reviews, assisting with failing CI, or helping to verify patches and add the `verified` label to the PR.

### Modified

Bugs move to this stage once all PRs are merged. They remain in this stage until a nightly build has been accepted containing the relevant fixes. There should be no action required for 99% of bugs in the modified stage. Occasionally bugs get stuck in this stage and may need a helping hand to move forward if they have not done so and a green nightly has been promoted containing all relevant PRs.

### ON\_QA

Most bugs should be verified before they are merged, when this happens, the bug will automatically progress to Verified. A small number will be `verified-later`, and those bugs must be handled in the ON\_QA phase. The RIT QA monitor should assess ON\_QA bugs that do not automatically progress to Verified and ensure that the bugs are still moving forward.

Automation will add the `post-merge-verification` label to any OCPBUGS issue identified as needing manual verification. Those needing attention can be seen in this [dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023#v=1&d=25023&rf=019df8d4-fead-7cda-9eea-99b816fd674b&smart=019e2bcc-ee24-786a-9eac-bee6db0f7a35:019e2bcd-411c-7cd3-89c6-7643e49eab31&g=97428:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97429:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97430:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97432:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97806:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97807:view@019e06bb-a647-70d3-8faf-37dbee373687;97810:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97813:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97816:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64).

Bugs in this phase typically fall into two buckets; they could not be pre-merge verified because of the complexity of merging many PRs; the user does not have access to the correct environments to be able to verify the bug.

In cases where the bug could not be verified due to complexity, the QA monitor should prompt the bug assignee to make sure they are now able to verify the issue. Verification ideally comes through the form of automated testing over manual testing.

When the bug assignee could not verify the issue because they lack access to environments, the QA monitor should assist in helping to find someone within the org who can either help provide access to the correct environment, or complete the verification on behalf of the bug assignee. 

Ultimately, the bug assignee is primarily responsible for making sure their bug is verified.

### Verified

The bug is now pending release. No further action is required by the RIT.

### Comment templates for status transitions

When changing a bug's status or assignee during triage, add a comment explaining the change. Use these templates:


**ASSIGNED — no linked PRs (ownership check):**
> RIT triage: this bug is in ASSIGNED status but has no linked PRs or visible code activity. If you are still actively working on this, no action is needed. If you are not intending to work on it, please move it back to New and unassign yourself so the next RIT rotation can pick it up.

**Setting priority (from Undefined):**
> RIT triage: setting priority to *{Priority}*. {One sentence reasoning — customer impact, severity, workaround availability.}

**PR-closed reset (Prow Bot):**
> RIT triage: this bug was automatically moved back to New when a linked PR was closed. Please take one of the following actions: (1) open a new PR, link it to this bug and update the status, or (2) close this ticket if the work is no longer being pursued.

**EOW cleanup — unassignment:**
> RIT end-of-week cleanup: this bug was not picked up during the current rotation. Removing the assignee so it can be reassessed and picked up by the next rotation.

**Sweep — stale triaged bug:**
> RIT health check: this bug has been triaged and assigned but has had no visible activity for {N} days. Please provide an update on the current status. If you are no longer working on this, please move it back to New and unassign yourself so it can be picked up.

## PIXAA bug triage process {#pixaa-bug-triage-process}

A PIXAA bug must be triaged when any of the following criteria are met:

* The bug is unassigned  
* The bug is missing a priority  
* The bug does not have the `triaged` label

Untriaged bugs can be viewed using this [dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023#v=1&d=25023&rf=019df8d4-fead-7cda-9eea-99b816fd674b&smart=019e0714-b7b0-70f6-afb4-e30e77023e91:019e0715-c022-7ce4-9dc3-d9c8762b836b&g=97428:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97429:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97430:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97432:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97806:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97807:view@019e06bb-a647-70d3-8faf-37dbee373687;97810:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97813:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97816:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64).

To triage a bug, you must assess:

* Is the bug component correctly assigned  
* Is the bug a release blocker  
* What is the priority of the bug  
* Who can take initial responsibility for investigation

Once all of the above have been assessed and set on the bug, add the `triaged` label and leave the bug in the `New` status.

### Assessing Component Assignment

Bugs are often assigned to components that are not the component that is actually affected. It is important that we correctly identify the bug component so that we can assess whether the bug should, or should not be investigated further by PIXAA.

Use the provided information in the bug to assess if the bug is obviously misaligned. If the correct component is not within the PIXAA org, make sure to add a comment explaining why you have transferred the issue to the new component before transferring.

If the issue is not obviously misaligned, assume it is correctly aligned and continue triage. The initial assigned engineer may find later that the component is misaligned, at which point they are expected to transfer and comment appropriately to explain why they think the new component is correct.

### Assessing Release Blocker

A release blocker bug delays shipping the upcoming OpenShift release. It is reserved for bugs that are high in severity and generally represent a regression in behaviour. The [formal definition](https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/blob/master/dev-guide/release-blocker-definition.md) for release blockers is documented in the dev-guide.

Once you have assessed, based on the [criteria](https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/blob/master/dev-guide/release-blocker-definition.md#when-to-set-release-blocker-to-approved-in-an-ocpbug), whether the bug is a release blocker or not, set the release blocker field to `Approved` or `Rejected` as appropriate. Where a blocker is identified, ensure the RIT lead is informed as they will want to track release blocker progress.  
![Mermaid flow sequence, sourced from https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVHSiwIhk=/?share\_link\_id=403840593961][image2]

### Assessing Priority

Bug priority ranges from least severe (Minor), through intermediate stages (Normal, Major) to the most severe at (Critical). The org uses the assessed priority to determine in which order bugs should be picked up.

Critical bugs should be picked up within a matter of days. Major bugs should be picked up within the sprint. Both Critical and Major bugs should take priority over feature work. Normal bugs should be prioritized among feature work each sprint. Minor bugs may be prioritized alongside feature work as and when capacity is available. If a bug remains Minor and unresolved for an extended period, consider closing it.

When determining priority, you should consider the following:

* Is this a CVE? It should normally be prioritized as Critical.  
* Is this a regression? Has the issue already shipped and are customers already affected?  
* Customer impact \- how many customers are impacted? What effect does the bug have on a customer’s cluster? Does it disrupt data flow or cause data loss?  
* Does a workaround exist? Is the workaround particularly complex?

![][image3]

### Assigning an Initial Engineer

The final stage in the triage process is to assign an initial engineer. This can be any member of the RIT with capacity (including yourself). The responsibility of the initial engineer is to make sure the bug has the right information to be able to reproduce the issue. This engineer should check if the bug is reproducible and whether a must-gather or any other relevant logs have been included.

The initial engineer should then also investigate the bug based on the information they have gathered and determine whether they are able to find the bug, and propose a fix, or whether the bug needs deeper SME knowledge or understanding. If the initial engineer has exhausted their, and their RIT team mates knowledge on an area and cannot identify the bug, they may escalate the bug to an SME in the area who can then take over the bug. This escalation should be a last resort.

To assign an initial engineer, consider the priority of the bug. Critical and Major bugs should be posted into \#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt channel to highlight to other RIT members that these need attention. Normal and Minor priority bugs can be left until the next daily standup.  
You may apply the `triaged` label before the assignee has been found if that helps filter out bugs that need the Triage monitors attention throughout the day. Use the `Hide Triaged (ignore assignee)` rich filter to hide triaged labelled bugs even if they don’t yet have an assignee. Switch to `Hide Triaged` to then show the bugs missing assignees when handling assignment to engineers.

### Useful Filter Combinations

The following filtering combinations may be useful on the [PIXXA Bugs board](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023#v=1&d=25023&rf=019df8d4-fead-7cda-9eea-99b816fd674b&smart=019e0714-b7b0-70f6-afb4-e30e77023e91:019e0715-c022-7ce4-9dc3-d9c8762b836b&g=97428:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97429:view@019df8e6-407e-70f8-b522-ae2fa478e0ff;97430:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97432:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97806:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97807:view@019e06bb-a647-70d3-8faf-37dbee373687;97810:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97813:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64;97816:view@019df8dd-217a-71da-ae6c-9e1851bf4a64).

* As bugs that are Unassigned are not considered triaged by the default filters, the following selections will show only those bugs that need attention (Priority, label, Blocker):  
  * Status \= ✔️New  
  * Assignee \= ✔️Unassigned  
  * Triaged \= ✔️Hide Triaged (ignore assignee)  
  * Sustaining \= ✔️Hide Sustaining  
* To find bugs that are available to take (to work on), they must be triaged but Unassigned:  
  * Status \= ✔️New  
  * Assignee \= ✔️Unassigned  
  * Triaged \= ✔️Show Triaged (ignore assignee)  
  * Sustaining \= ✔️Hide Sustaining

## Handling of pre-pixaa bugs

Pre-existing bugs will not align to the expectations of our PIXAA bug process. RIT leads and RIT members should in their day to day start to assess old pre-pixaa that do not currently have an assignee.

In particular, it may be helpful to assess bugs that have not been updated in the longest time should be untriaged and then re-triaged. Co-ordinate with existing bug owners to assess whether the bug is still relevant, adjust the priority and determine with the existing owner if they have invested sufficient time into the bug such that they should continue to own the bug moving forward, or whether it should be put into the org pool.

Longstanding **customer case bugs should be prioritised** in this process.

## Handling of CVEs

CVEs for many components under PIXAA will be handled by the sustaining engineering team for all branches for GA releases. This means that the RIT is only responsible for triaging and fixing CVEs in the current development and pre-GA branches for these components.

Sustaining engineering bugs will appear by default on the PIXAA bugs [dashboard](https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/25023), however, they can be filtered with the “Sustaining” option under the Rich Filter Controller. Sustaining engineers should be able to self service their own bugs and they should not need attention from PIXAA engineers.

**Sustaining label automation lag** — The `ocp-sustaining` label is applied automatically by a bot, but this can take up to **one hour** after a bug is created. During that window, sustaining bugs may appear in the Untriaged panel without the label, causing them to be picked up by RIT triage in error. Bugs with `arc:*` labels (e.g. `arc:devel`) are a signal that the sustaining bot will act on the ticket. If a bug was created less than an hour ago and has `arc:*` labels, do not triage it — check back after the label has been applied.

For CVEs not handled by PIXAA, the RIT should aim to resolve these quickly. CVEs will have a due date assigned and we should endeavour to ensure that the due date is met for all CVEs. The due date is visible in the With Due Date panel of the PIXAA bugs dashboard.

CVE exposure is based on a package level analysis. In some cases, a symbol level analysis will show that the component is not actually exposed to the vulnerability. In these cases the package should still be updated, but not attached to the bug. This ensures that we pre-emptively fix a potential future exposure, but do not alert customers to a “fix” that actually didn’t change the exposure. The bug should be closed as Not A Bug.

## Handling of Embargoed CVEs

Bugs that are embargoed CVEs have limited visibility; only those people attached to the bug (e.g. as assignee, reporter or contributor) are able to view those tickets. The normal process of fixing upstream, downstreaming (to the pre-GA branch), and then backporting to sustaining branches needs to be modified in order to avoid exposing the embargoed CVE until it is lifted.

The RIT lead (managers) should be automatically added as a contributor to all embargoed CVEs. Talk to your RIT lead to request access.

Resources/Training for handling Embargoed CVEs:

* [Embargoed CVE Lifecycle & Team Workflow for OpenShift 4](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KuenDafC3Ukw19jY55tkVeH8nNVVAi8TEAfqynoVfzY/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.idxdm0f9cj2x)  
* [Red Hat Learning: Security Embargoes](https://training-lms.redhat.com/lmt/clmsCourseDetails.prMain?in_sessionId=58002J3989198A09&in_from_module=CLMSBROWSEV2.PRMAIN&in_offeringId=67888956)  
* [Product Security Documentation \- Embargo Standard \- Requires VPN](https://prodsec.pages.redhat.com/prodsec-docs/policies/embargo-standard/)  
* [Product Security Documentation \- Embargo Access Control Process \- Requires VPN](https://prodsec.pages.redhat.com/prodsec-docs/incident-response/Embargo_Process/)

## Workflows

Support channels will be set to a workflow-by-default conversation style. This prompts forum users to fill out a template to provide detail on their ask, rather than posting an unstructured message. Unstructured messages will still be allowed, but will not escalate to the RIT automatically.

The workflows will first prompt the chai-bot to respond to requests. The person requesting support then has an option to request human help. This will then trigger a message in the **\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt** channel pinging the **@pixaa-slack-monitor** alias (see [Slack Monitor](#slack-monitor)) who will then be responsible for finding an appropriate assignee to assist with the request.

# FAQ

# FAQ

### I’m on the RIT, what should I be spending my time doing?

Depending on whether you have been assigned one of [the rotational team roles]() (e.g. Triage or Slack monitor), you will either focus primarily on this rotational role, with a secondary focus on fixing bugs, or, your primary focus will be investigating and fixing bugs for the week.

Where escalations need synchronous attention, you may be asked to park bugs in favour of higher priority escalations.

### I have exhausted my knowledge in a component area, how do I escalate to an SME?

Firstly, check within the RIT. Use the [\#forum-ocp-pixaa-interrupt](https://redhat.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0B2C9VAHLK) to see if any of the members of the RIT are able to help unblock you. If not, they may have a suggestion for an SME to escalate to.

As a second option, check the [CCSIGs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bXGksEjpSjnFcrKt3Aln9dIQXF02_jfX5B0tInJChZY/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.zd3xlp469xk0). One of the CCSIGs may align to the component area you are stuck on. The CCSIGs will have an internal channel that you can join and ask questions in to help find the expertise you need.

If the above fails, the OWNERS files in the repository root will generally have a list of names of approvers. These names are generally SMEs in the area.

If all else fails, request assistance from someone in [the Red Dragon pod](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/u/0/d/1XHWfuJJTTouvQXiApzdiT6H09cwHsDJGbqdzXFl1-4s/edit) who will help to find you an SME.

### I have an idea to improve part of the RIT process, how can I move that idea forward?

The RIT is intended to be a continually evolving process. Only through actually being on RIT will we learn where there are rough edges in the processes. Initially, we expect the processes to suck. While on RIT, even beyond, if you have ideas for improving the process, you are welcome to implement them. Scripts, agentic skills and any other tools you want to build for the RIT can be shared through the [openshift-eng/pixaa](https://github.com/openshift-eng/pixaa) repository.

If you have larger process changes you’d like to suggest, there will be a RIT retrospective periodically (initially every 6 weeks) open to all PIXAA engineers, or you can discuss with your manager or [a Red Dragon pod engineer](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/u/0/d/1XHWfuJJTTouvQXiApzdiT6H09cwHsDJGbqdzXFl1-4s/edit).

### I have feedback about the RIT, who can I talk to?

All managers under Chris, and the engineers of the Red Dragon pod have been involved in the building of this process. Feel free to provide feedback to any of them. 

There will also be a retrospective set up, initially every 6 weeks with an open invite to allow a dedicated space to provide feedback on the process and talk about things that have been going well, or not so well.

The RIT is expected to evolve over time. If you have feedback and feel like you can action it and improve the process, we would like you to own that.

## Access AWS/GCP/Azure/vSphere

New accounts have been provisioned on each platform specifically for PIXAA. The intention of these cloud accounts is to consolidate. So we expect old accounts to be decommissioned soon. All of these accounts have pruning enabled, though we can opt out of pruning for certain resources, or resource groups depending on the cloud.

If you have long lived resources in existing accounts, please reach out to [Joel Speed](mailto:jspeed@redhat.com)

#### AWS

To access AWS, search [Rover apps](https://rover.redhat.com/apps/#IT) for AWS and this will take you to an [SSO page to login](https://auth.redhat.com/auth/realms/EmployeeIDP/protocol/saml/clients/itaws). You can then choose the poweruser role under the new PIXAA-dev account (359703527040). Everyone under Chris Alfonso automatically has access to this account.

#### GCP

To access GCP, launch [console.cloud.google.com](http://console.cloud.google.com) , on the top left select [the PIXAA dev project](https://console.cloud.google.com/welcome?project=pixaa-dev) in the project picker. Everyone under Chris Alfonso automatically has access to this account.

#### Azure

To access Azure, login to the [azure portal](http://portal.azure.com), switch to the "PNT Cloud Ops Dev/Test" tenant. This will grant you access to the PIXAA Dev subscription. Access to Azure is manual, anyone new to the org must contact [a red dragon engineer](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1XHWfuJJTTouvQXiApzdiT6H09cwHsDJGbqdzXFl1-4s/edit?gid=0#gid=0) to be added to the Entra ID group that permits access.

##### Adding a member to the PIXAA Azure subscription

1. Open the [azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/), navigate to the Mircosoft Entra ID service.  
2. This should open a page with a panel to the left, select Manage \> Groups.  
3. A search box “search your tennant” appears, type PIXAA and click on “PIXAA Dev” when it appears.  
4. On the new page, Manage \> Members.  
5. Click “Add members” towards the top of this view  
6. Search for the user(s) you want to add and tick the corresponding account  
7. Hit “Select” at the bottom of this pane  
8. Users are now added to the Entra ID group which will grant them access to our subscription

#### vSphere

vSphere access must be individually requested when required. Review the [onboarding doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cnzKMT-8TGcq5ox_AajGpT-VRwMuYTKIZI-fPNrR8Xg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.pt8d46lus3jk) for access and then the [cluster bootstrapping](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ltRPOubbwvteQy-sXP9Vwj2y6IoIKBUYskeJCRYaj7A/edit?usp=sharing) doc for creating a cluster.

## Bootstrapping Clusters

### Common

Steps needed for bootstrapping clusters on any platform

#### Pull Secret

Fetch the core pull-secret from [console.redhat.com](https://console.redhat.com/openshift/install/pull-secret). This pull secret contains credentials for core registries needed to pull production OpenShift payload images.  
For development and test, you’ll want to supplement this with the pull-secret for [`registry.ci.openshift.org`](http://registry.ci.openshift.org) and possibly other repositories.

Login to the [registry.ci.openshift.org](https://oauth-openshift.apps.ci.l2s4.p1.openshiftapps.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=openshift-browser-client&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Foauth-openshift.apps.ci.l2s4.p1.openshiftapps.com%2Foauth%2Ftoken%2Fdisplay&response_type=code) cluster and hit “Display Token”.  
Use the displayed `oc login` command to login to the cluster.

Use `oc registry login –to=registry.json` to dump a partial pull-secret.  
Merge the contents of this partial pull-secret with the content downloaded from [`console.redhat.com`](http://console.redhat.com).

The registry authentication will need to be re-authenticated periodically.

#### Release Images

OpenShift cluster CI, Nightly, EC builds can be sourced from the [Release Status](https://amd64.ocp.releases.ci.openshift.org/) dashboard.  
By clicking on a particular release you will see a list of jobs that ran (informing and blocking) against that payload, and also have the ability to view new changes against previous releases.

##### Extracting the installer binaries

At the top of a particular release page, you will see a command that looks approximately like

```shell
oc adm release extract --tools registry.ci.openshift.org/ocp/release-5:5.0.0-0.nightly-2026-05-29-064906
```

Tips:

* Substitute `--tools` for `--command openshift-install` or other specific command if you only need one tool  
* Use the `-a` flag to point to your pull-secret, e.g. `-a pull-secret.txt`  
* Always extract a new `openshift-install` daily using your pull secret  
  * This means you know the payload images are still present  
  * It also tests that your pull secret is still valid

### AWS

#### Create a user

Login to the [AWS console via SSO](https://auth.redhat.com/auth/realms/EmployeeIDP/protocol/saml/clients/itaws). Select the `359703527040-openshift-installer-restricted` role to login.

Navigate to IAM \> IAM Users. Create a user with the name matching your kerberos ID. When prompted, add the user to the `openshift-installer` group to set the correct permissions.

Once the user is created, select the user and native to the `Security Credentials` tab. Create an access key and note the key ID and secret access key.

You will need to create `~/.aws/credentials` locally if it does not exist. This is an `ini` formatted file containing credential profiles.

Add a section as below:

```
[pixaa-dev]
aws_access_key_id = <key you just created>
aws_secret_access_key = <secret you just created>
```

Ensure the AWS SDK picks this up as your default profile `export AWS_PROFILE=pixaa-dev`. Add this to whichever shell profile you use.

#### Creating the cluster

Use your `openshift-install` binary to create the cluster. 

```shell
openshift-install create cluster --dir <cluster-dir>
```

It will prompt for the platform, and then the region. It is recommended to NOT use `us-east-1` even though it is the default. `Us-east-1` has 6 availability zones and therefore requires 6 copies of the AWS networking infrastructure (network gateways). This means these clusters are more expensive than using a region that only uses 3 availability zones. `Us-east-2` is a good default for creating clusters unless you need a specific region.

When prompted for a name, please include your kerberos ID as a cluster name prefix.

##### Tearing down the cluster

Use your `openshift-install` binary to destroy the cluster.  
If your cluster was created more than 12 hours ago, some resources will already have been pruned by the account automatic pruning. It is still recommended to run the destroy to clean up remaining resources such as IAM and Route53 records.

```shell
openshift-install dest	roy cluster --dir <cluster-dir>
```

### Cincinnati

Cincinnati is a service powering OpenShift updates. Data about version support is located in [https://github.com/openshift/cincinnati-graph-data](https://github.com/openshift/cincinnati-graph-data/blob/master/OWNERS_ALIASES).

PRs that add a supported upgrade version are created and merged automatically. If any of these promotions fail, take action as soon as possible; Cincinnati is a time-sensitive pipeline. If you do not have permissions to resolve conflicts in the GitHub UI, open a PR and ping someone listed in [https://github.com/openshift/cincinnati-graph-data/blob/master/OWNERS\_ALIASES](https://github.com/openshift/cincinnati-graph-data/blob/master/OWNERS_ALIASES).
